Reciprocals of Subsum Polynomials

Cristina Ballantine Address: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science
College of the Holy Cross
Worcester, MA 01610, USA Email address: cballant@holycross.edu , George Beck Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics

Abstract.

We introduce the subsum polynomial of a partition λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) defined by sp⁡(λ,x)=∏i=1k(1+xλi)\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1+x^{\lambda_{i}}). We study the sum of reciprocals of sp⁡(λ,x)\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x) over all partitions of nn. We prove arithmetic properties of related polynomials and offer connections to other combinatorial objects.

Key words and phrases:
integer partitions, polynomial defined by partition, sum of reciprocals of polynomials
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11R09, 11P81, 05A17, 11A05

1. Introduction

An integer partition λ\lambda of nn is a nonincreasing sequence λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}) of positive integers that add up to nn. We write λ⊢n\lambda\vdash n to mean that λ\lambda is a partition of nn. The numbers λi\lambda_{i} in the sequence are called the parts of λ\lambda. We identify a partition with its multiset of parts. We denote by P⁡(n)P(n) the number of partitions of nn and set P⁡(0):=1P(0):=1. We occasionally use the frequency notation of partitions. Exponents of parts represent their multiplicity. For example, (32,24,12)(3^{2},2^{4},1^{2}) is the partition (3,3,2,2,2,2,1,1)(3,3,2,2,2,2,1,1). For more on the theory of partitions, we refer the reader to [1].

Given a partition λ=(λ1,λ2,…,λk)\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\ldots,\lambda_{k}), we define the polynomial

sp⁡(λ,x):=∏i=1k(1+xλi).\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x):=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(1+x^{\lambda_{i}}).

In analogy with the generating function for the number of partitions with distinct parts, we can view the polynomial sp⁡(λ,x)\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x) as the generating function for the number of partitions whose parts form a submultiset of λ\lambda. This inspired the name subsum polynomial for sp⁡(λ,x)\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x). This construction is also reminiscent of Stanton’s polynomial GλG_{\lambda}, the generating function of all partitions that lie inside of λ\lambda (see [7]). Clearly, if λ\lambda is a partition of nn, then deg⁡(sp⁡(λ,x))=n\deg(\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x))=n.

If mλ​(i)m_{\lambda}(i) denotes the number of times ii occurs as a part in λ\lambda, then

sp⁡(λ,x)=∏i=1n(1+xi)mλ​(i).\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+x^{i})^{m_{\lambda}(i)}.

Numerical experimentation led us to define and study the rational function

sr⁡(n,x):=∑λ⊢n1sp⁡(λ,x).\mathrm{sr}(n,x):=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\frac{1}{\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)}.

For any partition λ⊢n\lambda\vdash n, let

hλ​(x):=∏i≥1(1+xi)⌊n/i⌋−mλ​(i).h_{\lambda}(x):=\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x^{i})^{\lfloor n/i\rfloor-m_{\lambda}(i)}\>.

We define

num∗​(n,x):=∑λ⊢nhλ​(x)\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x):=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}h_{\lambda}(x)

and

den∗​(n,x):=∏i≥1(1+xi)⌊n/i⌋.\mathrm{den}^{*}(n,x):=\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x^{i})^{\lfloor n/i\rfloor}\>.

Then,

sr⁡(n,x)=num∗​(n,x)den∗​(n,x).\mathrm{sr}(n,x)=\frac{\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x)}{\mathrm{den}^{*}(n,x)}.

We can also write

num∗​(n,x)=∑μ⊢∑i=1nσ1​(i)−nmμ​(i)≤⌊ni⌋sp⁡(μ,x),\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\vdash\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{1}(i)-n\\ m_{\mu}(i)\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor\end{subarray}}\mathrm{sp}(\mu,x),

where σ1​(i)\sigma_{1}(i) denotes the sum of divisors of ii.

The degree of den∗​(n,x)\mathrm{den}^{*}(n,x) is ∑i=1ni⁡⌊n/i⌋=∑i=1nσ1​(i)\sum_{i=1}^{n}i\lfloor n/i\rfloor=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{1}(i). This is sequence A024916 in OEIS [5]. We have

deg⁡(hλ​(x))\displaystyle\deg(h_{\lambda}(x)) =∑i=1nσ1​(i)−∑i=1ni​mλ​(i)=∑i=1nσ1​(i)−n=deg⁡(num∗​(n,x)).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{1}(i)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}im_{\lambda}(i)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{1}(i)-n=\deg(\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x)).

Thus

deg⁡(den∗​(n,x))−deg⁡(num∗​(n,x))=n.\deg(\mathrm{den}^{*}(n,x))-\deg(\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x))=n.

Next, we define

G(n,x):=gcd{hλ(x)∣λ⊢n},G(n,x):=\gcd\{h_{\lambda}(x)\mid\lambda\vdash n\}\>,

and let

num⁡(n,x):=num∗​(n,x)G⁡(n,x) and den⁡(n,x):=den∗​(n,x)G⁡(n,x).\mathrm{num}(n,x):=\frac{\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x)}{G(n,x)}\quad\textrm{ and }\quad\mathrm{den}(n,x):=\frac{\mathrm{den}^{*}(n,x)}{G(n,x)}\>.

In Section 3 we prove results about num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x) and den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x). Below we list some of them.

A polynomial is palindromic if its coefficients form a palindrome. A sequence u1,u2,…,umu_{1},u_{2},\ldots,u_{m} of real numbers is said to be unimodal if, for some jj, u1≤u2≤…≤uj≥uj+1≥…≥umu_{1}\leq u_{2}\leq\ldots\leq u_{j}\geq u_{j+1}\geq\ldots\geq u_{m}. A polynomial is unimodal if its sequence of coefficients is unimodal.

Proposition (3.9).

Let nn be a positive integer. Then,

  1. (a)

    G⁡(n,x)G(n,x), num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x), and den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) are palindromic.

  2. (b)

    den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) and G⁡(n,x)G(n,x) are unimodal.

Theorem (3.18).

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

  1. (a)

    num⁡(n,−1)=n!\mathrm{num}(n,-1)=n!

  2. (b)

    |num⁡(n,±i)|=2⌊n/2⌋​⌊n/2⌋!\lvert\mathrm{num}(n,\pm\mathrm{i})\rvert=2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\lfloor n/2\rfloor!

  3. (c)

    |num⁡(n,ζ6)|={3⌊n/3⌋​⌊n/3⌋!n≢2(mod3)4⋅3⌊n/3⌋​⌊n/3⌋!n≡2(mod3),\lvert\mathrm{num}(n,\zeta_{6})\rvert=\begin{cases}3^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}\lfloor n/3\rfloor!&n\not\equiv 2\pmod{3}\\ 4\cdot 3^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}\lfloor n/3\rfloor!&n\equiv 2\pmod{3},\end{cases}
    where ζ6\zeta_{6} is a primitive sixth root of unity.

Proposition (3.13).

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

  1. (a)

    den⁡(n,1)=2val2​((2​n)!)\mathrm{den}(n,1)=2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}((2n)!)},

  2. (b)

    num⁡(n,1)=2val2​(n!)​P​(n)\mathrm{num}(n,1)=2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n!)}P(n).

Numerical evidence suggests the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.

For n≥1n\geq 1, the polynomial num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x) is irreducible over the integers.

We also make a somewhat weaker claim for which we have achieved some partial results:

Conjecture 2.

For n≥1n\geq 1,

gcd⁡(num⁡(n,x),den⁡(n,x))=1.\gcd\bigl(\mathrm{num}(n,x),\mathrm{den}(n,x)\bigr)=1\>.

Conjecture 1 implies Conjecture 2 (see Remark 5).

In Section 4 we prove some analogous results for binary partitions, that is, partitions whose parts are powers of two. In Section 5, we briefly consider a generalization of sr⁡(n,x)\mathrm{sr}(n,x), namely ∑λ⊢nsp​(λ,x)m\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)^{m} for m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z}. In Section 6, we discuss open questions for sums of reciprocals of subsum polynomials defined on restricted sets of partitions.

2. Preliminaries

In this section we establish useful properties of polynomials of the form 1+xi1+x^{i}. For the convenience of the reader, we give complete proofs.

We write val2​(n)\mathrm{val}_{2}(n) for the 22-valuation of the integer nn. We denote by Φd​(x)\Phi_{d}(x) the dd-th cyclotomic polynomial, which is irreducible in ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x].

Remark 1.

Since xn−1=∏d|nΦd​(x)x^{n}-1=\prod_{d|n}\Phi_{d}(x) for any positive integer nn, and

x2​i−1=(xi−1)​(1+xi),x^{2i}-1=(x^{i}-1)(1+x^{i}),

it follows that

(1) (1+xi)=∏d|2​id∤iΦd​(x).(1+x^{i})=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d|2i\\ d\nmid i\end{subarray}}\Phi_{d}(x).
Lemma 2.1.

  1. (a)

    1+xi1+x^{i} is irreducible in ℤ⁡[x]\mathbb{Z}[x] if and only if i=2ki=2^{k} for some k≥0k\geq 0.

  2. (b)

    gcd⁡(1+xn,1+xm)={1, if ​val2​(n)≠val2​(m)1+xgcd⁡(n,m), if ​val2​(n)=val2​(m).\gcd(1+x^{n},1+x^{m})=\begin{cases}1,&\textrm{ if }\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)\neq\mathrm{val}_{2}(m)\\ 1+x^{\gcd(n,m)},&\textrm{ if }\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)=\mathrm{val}_{2}(m).\end{cases}

  3. (c)

    In particular, (1+xi)|(1+xm)(1+x^{i})\mid(1+x^{m}) if and only if m=i⋅jm=i\cdot j for some odd jj.

Proof.

(a) The statement holds because the right hand side of (1) has a single factor if and only if i=2ki=2^{k} for some k≥0k\geq 0.

(b) From (1), it follows that

(2) gcd⁡(1+xn,1+xm)=∏d|2⋅gcd⁡(n,m)d∤n,d∤mΦd​(x).\gcd(1+x^{n},1+x^{m})=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid 2\cdot\gcd(n,m)\\ d\nmid n,d\nmid m\end{subarray}}\Phi_{d}(x).

Clearly, each dd that occurs as an index in the product above satisfies d∤gcd⁡(n,m)d\nmid\gcd(n,m).

Case 1: val2​(n)≠val2​(m)\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)\neq\mathrm{val}_{2}(m). Assuming n>mn>m, let n=2j⋅a⋅gcd⁡(n,m)n=2^{j}\cdot a\cdot\gcd(n,m) and m=b⋅gcd⁡(n,m)m=b\cdot\gcd(n,m), where j>0j>0 and a,ba,b are odd. Then, if d|2⋅gcd⁡(n,m)d\mid 2\cdot\gcd(n,m) we have d|nd\mid n. Hence, the product in (2) is empty and gcd⁡(1+xn,1+xm)=1\gcd(1+x^{n},1+x^{m})=1.

Case 2: val2​(n)=val2​(m)\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)=\mathrm{val}_{2}(m). Let n=a⋅gcd⁡(n,m)n=a\cdot\gcd(n,m) and m=b⋅gcd⁡(n,m)m=b\cdot\gcd(n,m), where a,ba,b are odd. Then for each dd such that d|2⋅gcd⁡(n,m)d\mid 2\cdot\gcd(n,m) but d∤gcd⁡(n,m)d\nmid\gcd(n,m) we have val2​(d)=val2​(gcd⁡(n,m))+1=val2​(n)+1=val2​(m)+1\mathrm{val}_{2}(d)=\mathrm{val}_{2}(\gcd(n,m))+1=\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)+1=\mathrm{val}_{2}(m)+1, that is, d∤nd\nmid n and d∤md\nmid m. We may rewrite (2) as

gcd⁡(1+xn,1+xm)=∏d|2⋅gcd⁡(n,m)d∤gcd⁡(n,m)Φd​(x)=1+xgcd⁡(n,m).\gcd(1+x^{n},1+x^{m})=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid 2\cdot\gcd(n,m)\\ d\nmid\gcd(n,m)\end{subarray}}\Phi_{d}(x)=1+x^{\gcd(n,m)}.

(c) Notice that (1+xi)|(1+xm)(1+x^{i})\mid(1+x^{m}) is equivalent to (1+xi)=gcd⁡(1+xi,1+xm)(1+x^{i})=\gcd(1+x^{i},1+x^{m}), which by part (b) holds if and only if val2​(i)=val2​(m)\mathrm{val}_{2}(i)=\mathrm{val}_{2}(m) and i=gcd⁡(i,m)i=\gcd(i,m), that is, if and only if m=i⋅jm=i\cdot j for some odd jj. ∎

Remark 2.

If i=ℓ⋅ji=\ell\cdot j with odd jj, we have the factorization

1+xi=(1+xℓ)⋅∑k=0j−1(−xℓ)k=(1+xℓ)​(xℓ⁡(j−1)−xℓ⁡(j−2)+…−xℓ+1).1+x^{i}=(1+x^{\ell})\cdot\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}(-x^{\ell})^{k}=(1+x^{\ell})(x^{\ell(j-1)}-x^{\ell(j-2)}+\ldots-x^{\ell}+1).
Corollary 2.2.

The gcd\gcd of any finite collection of products of terms of the form (1+xi)(1+x^{i}) can be written as a product of terms of the form (1+xj)(1+x^{j}). In particular, G⁡(n,x)G(n,x) decomposes into the product

G(n,x)=∏j=0⌊log2⁡(n)⌋gcd{∏d≥1,d​ odd(1+x2j​d)⌊n2j​d⌋−mλ​(2j​d)∣λ⊢n}.G(n,x)=\prod_{j=0}^{\lfloor\log_{2}(n)\rfloor}\gcd\{\prod_{d\geq 1,d\textrm{ odd}}(1+x^{2^{j}d})^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{j}d}\rfloor-m_{\lambda}(2^{j}d)}\mid\lambda\vdash n\}.

We also recall basic facts about palindromic and unimodal polynomials.

Remark 3.

  1. (a)

    Products and quotients of palindromic polynomials are palindromic and sums of palindromic polynomials of the same degree are palindromic. In particular, for all i,ℓ≥1i,\ell\geq 1, the polynomial (1+xi)ℓ(1+x^{i})^{\ell} is palindromic.

  2. (b)

    A product of palindromic, unimodal polynomials is again unimodal [2].

3. Ordinary partitions

Recall that

hλ​(x)=∏i≥1(1+xi)⌊n/i⌋−mλ​(i).h_{\lambda}(x)=\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x^{i})^{\lfloor n/i\rfloor-m_{\lambda}(i)}.

By Lemma 2.1 (or also by Corollary 2.2) there exists a product decomposition of G(n,x)=gcd{hλ(x)∣λ⊢n}G(n,x)=\gcd\{h_{\lambda}(x)\mid\lambda\vdash n\} as

(3) G⁡(n,x)=∏i≥1(1+xi)cn,i.G(n,x)=\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x^{i})^{c_{n,i}}\>.

Note that this is not a decomposition into coprime factors. Our next goal is to understand the exponents cn,ic_{n,i}. We first introduce more notation. Given a positive integer nn, for each i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, we define γn,i\gamma_{n,i} as the maximal non-negative integer such that

(1+xi)γn,i|G⁡(n,x).(1+x^{i})^{\gamma_{n,i}}\mid G(n,x)\>.

Clearly, cn,i≤γn,ic_{n,i}\leq\gamma_{n,i}.

The next lemma can be used to determine the coefficients cn,ic_{n,i} recursively for fixed nn.

Lemma 3.1.

With the notation above, for n≥1n\geq 1 we have

  1. (a)

    For all i≥1i\geq 1,

    γn,i=∑j≥1​ oddcn,i⋅j=∑j>1​ odd⌊ni⋅j⌋.\gamma_{n,i}=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}c_{n,i\cdot j}=\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor\>.
  2. (b)

    For i>⌊n3⌋i>\lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor, cn,i=γn,i=0c_{n,i}=\gamma_{n,i}=0.

  3. (c)

    For 3​i>⌊n3⌋≥i3i>\lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor\geq i, cn,i=γn,ic_{n,i}=\gamma_{n,i}.

Proof.

These are consequences of Lemma 2.1: The term (1+xi)(1+x^{i}) divides (1+xk)(1+x^{k}) if and only if k=i⋅jk=i\cdot j for some odd j≥1j\geq 1, and if so, the multiplicity of (1+xi)(1+x^{i}) in the decomposition of (1+xk)(1+x^{k}) is one.

(a) For any ii, we have γn,i=∑j≥1​ oddcn,i⋅j\gamma_{n,i}=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}c_{n,i\cdot j}. On the other hand, since

hλ​(x)=∏i≥1(1+xi)⌊n/i⌋−mλ​(i),h_{\lambda}(x)=\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x^{i})^{\lfloor n/i\rfloor-m_{\lambda}(i)}\>,

we also have

γn,i=minλ⊢n⁡(∑j​ odd(⌊ni⋅j⌋−mλ​(i⋅j))).\gamma_{n,i}=\min_{\lambda\vdash n}\left(\sum_{j\textrm{ odd}}(\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor-m_{\lambda}(i\cdot j))\right)\>.

The sum on the right hand side is minimal for each λ\lambda such that mλ​(i)=⌊ni⌋m_{\lambda}(i)=\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor and for such a λ\lambda we have mλ​(i⋅j)=0m_{\lambda}(i\cdot j)=0 for all j>1j>1. The minimality claim holds because, if λ\lambda has mλ​(i)<⌊ni⌋m_{\lambda}(i)<\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor, then

∑j>1mλ​(i⋅j)<∑j>1j​mλ​(i⋅j)≤⌊ni⌋−mλ​(i).\sum_{j>1}m_{\lambda}(i\cdot j)<\sum_{j>1}jm_{\lambda}(i\cdot j)\leq\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-m_{\lambda}(i).

Partitions λ\lambda with mλ​(i)=⌊ni⌋m_{\lambda}(i)=\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor exist, for example λ=(i⌊ni⌋,1n−⌊ni⌋)\lambda=(i^{\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor},1^{n-\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor}). Hence, we obtain

γn,i=∑j>1​ odd⌊ni⋅j⌋.\gamma_{n,i}=\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor.

(b) If i>⌊n/3⌋i>\lfloor n/3\rfloor, there is no multiple kk of ii satisfying n≥k=i⋅j>in\geq k=i\cdot j>i with jj odd. So by (a), 0=∑j>1​ odd⌊ni⋅j⌋=γn,i=cn,i0=\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor=\gamma_{n,i}=c_{n,i}.

(c) For 3​i>⌊n3⌋≥i3i>\lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor\geq i by (a) and (b), γn,i=∑j≥1​ oddcn,i⋅j=cn,i\gamma_{n,i}=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}c_{n,i\cdot j}=c_{n,i}. ∎

For each i≥1i\geq 1, (1+xi)γn,i|num∗​(n,x)(1+x^{i})^{\gamma_{n,i}}\mid\mathrm{num}^{*}(n,x) and γn,i\gamma_{n,i} is the largest such power as shown below.

Lemma 3.2.

Let p⁡(x)=∏i=1N(1+xi)aip(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1+x^{i})^{a_{i}} and q⁡(x)=∏i=1N(1+xi)biq(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1+x^{i})^{b_{i}} be polynomials with exponents ai,bi≥0a_{i},b_{i}\geq 0. Let αi\alpha_{i} (resp. βi\beta_{i}) be the maximal exponent such that (1+xi)αi|p⁡(x)(1+x^{i})^{\alpha_{i}}\mid p(x) (resp. (1+xi)βi|q⁡(x)(1+x^{i})^{\beta_{i}}\mid q(x)). If αi=βi\alpha_{i}=\beta_{i} for all ii, then p⁡(x)=q⁡(x)p(x)=q(x).

Proof.

Because αi=∑j≥1​ oddai⋅j\alpha_{i}=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}a_{i\cdot j} (resp. βi=∑j≥1​ oddbi⋅j\beta_{i}=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}b_{i\cdot j}), and because αi=ai\alpha_{i}=a_{i} (resp. βi=bi\beta_{i}=b_{i}) for i>⌊N/3⌋i>\lfloor N/3\rfloor, we obtain the coefficients aia_{i} (resp. bib_{i}) from the αi\alpha_{i} (resp. βi\beta_{i}) by recursion. So if αi=βi\alpha_{i}=\beta_{i} for all ii, then ai=bia_{i}=b_{i} for all ii. ∎

Using the results of the previous two lemmas, we prove the following about the quotients of G⁡(n,x)G(n,x) for consecutive values of nn. We use the notation

𝔮​G​(n,x):=G⁡(n,x)G⁡(n−1,x).\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}G}(n,x):=\frac{G(n,x)}{G(n-1,x)}\>.

For a positive integer mm, we denote by 𝐨⁡(m)\mathbf{o}(m) the largest odd divisor of mm, that is,

𝐨⁡(m)=m2val2​(m).\mathbf{o}(m)=\frac{m}{2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(m)}}.
Proposition 3.3.

Let n>1n>1. Then

𝔮​G​(n,x)=∏d|n𝐨⁡(n)∤d(1+xd),\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}G}(n,x)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\ \mathbf{o}(n)\nmid d\end{subarray}}(1+x^{d})\>,

In particular, if n=2kn=2^{k} then 𝔮​G​(n,x)=1\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}G}(n,x)=1.

Proof.

Define

χ⁡(n,k):={1 if ​k|n0 else, \chi(n,k):=\begin{cases}1&\textrm{ if }k\mid n\\ 0&\textrm{ else, }\end{cases}\>

so that ⌊nk⌋=⌊n−1k⌋+χ⁡(n,k)\lfloor\frac{n}{k}\rfloor=\lfloor\frac{n-1}{k}\rfloor+\chi(n,k). By Lemma 3.1, for the maximal exponents γn,i\gamma_{n,i} such that (1+xi)γn,i|G⁡(n,x)(1+x^{i})^{\gamma_{n,i}}\mid G(n,x) we have

γn,i=∑j>1​ odd⌊ni⋅j⌋=γn−1,i+∑j>1​ oddχ⁡(n,i⋅j).\gamma_{n,i}=\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor=\gamma_{n-1,i}+\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\chi(n,i\cdot j)\>.

For each 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, let δn,i\delta_{n,i} be the maximal exponent such that (1+xi)δn,i|∏d|n𝐨⁡(n)∤d(1+xd)(1+x^{i})^{\delta_{n,i}}\mid\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\ \mathbf{o}(n)\nmid d\end{subarray}}(1+x^{d}). Then we have

δn,i=∑j≥1​ odd i⋅j≠2val2​(i)−val2​(n)​nχ⁡(n,i⋅j)=∑j>1​ oddχ⁡(n,i⋅j).\delta_{n,i}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\geq 1\textrm{ odd }\\ i\cdot j\neq 2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(i)-\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)}n\end{subarray}}\chi(n,i\cdot j)=\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\chi(n,i\cdot j).

The last equality holds because both sides have the same number of summands with value 11 (and all other summands are zero).

So the maximal exponents ηn,i\eta_{n,i} such that (1+xi)ηn,i|∏d|n𝐨⁡(n)∤d(1+xd)⋅G⁡(n−1,x)(1+x^{i})^{\eta_{n,i}}\mid\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\ \mathbf{o}(n)\nmid d\end{subarray}}(1+x^{d})\cdot G(n-1,x) are

ηn,i=δn,i+γn−1,i=γn,i.\eta_{n,i}=\delta_{n,i}+\gamma_{n-1,i}=\gamma_{n,i}\>.

By Lemma 3.2, we have G⁡(n,x)=∏d|n𝐨⁡(n)∤d(1+xd)⋅G⁡(n−1,x)G(n,x)=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}d\mid n\\ \mathbf{o}(n)\nmid d\end{subarray}}(1+x^{d})\cdot G(n-1,x). ∎

Next, we examine the coefficients cn,ic_{n,i} in

G⁡(n,x)=∏i=1⌊n3⌋(1+xi)cn,i.G(n,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor}(1+x^{i})^{c_{n,i}}.

Let cn:=(cn,1,cn,2,…,cn,n)c_{n}:=(c_{n,1},c_{n,2},\ldots,c_{n,n}). By Lemma 3.1, we have cn,i=0c_{n,i}=0 if i>⌊n3⌋i>\lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor.

In the proof of our result we make use of the following identity for b=2b=2.

Lemma 3.4.

For all positive integers mm and any integral base b>1b>1 we have

m=∑j=1,b∤jm⌊logb⁡(b​mj)⌋.m=\sum_{{j=1,\,b\nmid j}}^{m}\lfloor\log_{b}(\frac{bm}{j})\rfloor.
Proof.

We prove this statement by induction on mm. When m=1m=1, both sides of the equation are 11. For the induction step notice that ⌊logb⁡(b⁡(m+1)j)⌋=⌊logb⁡(b​mj)⌋\lfloor\log_{b}(\frac{b(m+1)}{j})\rfloor=\lfloor\log_{b}(\frac{bm}{j})\rfloor unless b⁡(m+1)j=bk\frac{b(m+1)}{j}=b^{k} for some k>0k>0. But there is a unique j≤m+1j\leq m+1 with b∤jb\nmid j that satisfies this condition. So, by the induction hypothesis,

∑j=1,b∤jm+1⌊logb⁡(b⁡(m+1)j)⌋=m+1.\sum_{{j=1,\,b\nmid j}}^{m+1}\lfloor\log_{b}(\frac{b(m+1)}{j})\rfloor=m+1\>.

∎

Proposition 3.5.

Let nn be a positive integer.

  1. (a)

    For 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

    cn,i=⌊ni⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋−1.c_{n,i}=\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor-1\>.
  2. (b)

    cn,i>0c_{n,i}>0 for i=1,…,⌊n/3⌋i=1,\ldots,\lfloor n/3\rfloor, and cnc_{n} is weakly decreasing.

Proof.

(a) We show that ⌊ni⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋−1\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor-1 satisfies (a)–(c) of Lemma 3.1. That is, cn,ic_{n,i} and ⌊ni⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋−1\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor-1 satisfy the same recursion with the same initial conditions and thus must be equal. For i>⌊n3⌋i>\lfloor\frac{n}{3}\rfloor, obviously ⌊ni⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋−1=0\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor-1=0. Integers n,in,i satisfying 3​i>⌊n/3⌋≥i3i>\lfloor n/3\rfloor\geq i are related by n=a​i+rn=ai+r with 0≤r<i0\leq r<i and a∈{3,4,…,8}a\in\{3,4,\ldots,8\}. For those

cn,i=γn,i=⌊n3​i⌋+⌊n5​i⌋+⌊n7​i⌋=⌊a3⌋+⌊a5⌋+⌊a7⌋,c_{n,i}=\gamma_{n,i}=\lfloor\frac{n}{3i}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{n}{5i}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{n}{7i}\rfloor=\lfloor\frac{a}{3}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{a}{5}\rfloor+\lfloor\frac{a}{7}\rfloor\>,

and

⌊ni⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋−1=a−⌊log2⁡(a)⌋−1.\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor-1=a-\lfloor\lb(a)\rfloor-1\>.

We check case-by-case the claim cn,i=a−⌊log2⁡(a)⌋−1c_{n,i}=a-\lfloor\lb(a)\rfloor-1 holds for a∈{3,…,8}a\in\{3,\ldots,8\}. So ⌊ni⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋−1\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor-1 satisfies (b) and (c) of Lemma 3.1. Next we check that it satisfies the identity in (a) of Lemma 3.1, that is, we show

∑j≥1​ odd⌊n/i⌋(⌊ni⋅j⌋−⌊log2⁡(ni⋅j)⌋−1)=∑j>1​ odd⌊ni⋅j⌋,for alln≥i.\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}^{\lfloor n/i\rfloor}(\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor-\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i\cdot j})\rfloor-1)=\sum_{j>1\textrm{ odd}}\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor,\ \ \text{for all}\ \ n\geq i\>.

The above identity is equivalent to the following statement.

⌊ni⌋=∑j≥1​ odd⌊ni⌋(⌊log2⁡(⌊ni⋅j⌋)⌋+1),for alln≥i,\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor}(\lfloor\lb(\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor)\rfloor+1),\ \ \text{for all}\ \ n\geq i\>,

which is true by Lemma 3.4. This finishes the proof for (a).

(b) The statement follows immediately from (a). It can also be deduced from Lemma 3.1. ∎

Corollary 3.6.

The number of 11’s in cnc_{n} is ⌊n/3⌋−⌊n/5⌋\lfloor n/3\rfloor-\lfloor n/5\rfloor.

More generally,

  1. (a)

    if j=2t−t−1j=2^{t}-t-1 for some t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, then the number of entries equal to jj in cnc_{n} is ⌊n2t−1⌋−⌊n2t+1⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{t}-1}\rfloor-\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{t}+1}\rfloor,

  2. (b)

    if j≠2t−t−1j\neq 2^{t}-t-1 for any t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, then the number of entries equal to jj in cnc_{n} is ⌊nj+t0⌋−⌊nj+t0+1⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{j+t_{0}}\rfloor-\lfloor\frac{n}{j+t_{0}+1}\rfloor, where t0∈ℕt_{0}\in\mathbb{N} is such that 2t0−t0−1<j<2t0+1−(t0+1)−12^{t_{0}}-t_{0}-1<j<2^{t_{0}+1}-(t_{0}+1)-1.

Proof.

Using Proposition 3.5, one can check directly that cn,i=1c_{n,i}=1 if and only if ⌊n/i⌋∈{3,4}\lfloor n/i\rfloor\in\{3,4\}, that is, n/5<i≤n/3n/5<i\leq n/3. Then the number of 11’s in cnc_{n} is ⌊n/3⌋−⌊n/5⌋\lfloor n/3\rfloor-\lfloor n/5\rfloor. The general statement is proved similarly. ∎

We denote by σ0​(n)\sigma_{0}(n) the number of divisors of nn. Then, Proposition 3.5 leads to the following result on the number of factors of the form (1+xi)(1+x^{i}) in G⁡(n,x)G(n,x), counting multiplicities.

Corollary 3.7.

For positive integers nn, we have

log2⁡(G⁡(n,1))=∑i=1ncn,i=(∑i=1nσ0​(i))−val2​(n!)−n.\log_{2}(G(n,1))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{n,i}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{0}(i)\right)-\mathrm{val}_{2}(n!)-n.
Proof.

This follows immediately from Proposition 3.5(a),

∑i=1nσ0​(i)=∑i=1n⌊ni⌋​ and ​∑i=1n⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋=∑j=1nval2​(j)=val2​(n!).\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{0}(i)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor\text{\ \ \ \ and \ \ \ \ }\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathrm{val}_{2}(j)=\mathrm{val}_{2}(n!)\>.

The identity above on the right is true because for all k≥0k\geq 0,

#⁡{j≤n∣val2​(j)=k}=#⁡{i≤n∣⌊log2⁡(n/i)⌋=k}.\#\{j\leq n\mid\mathrm{val}_{2}(j)=k\}=\#\{i\leq n\mid\lfloor\lb(n/i)\rfloor=k\}\>.

∎

Using Legendre’s formula val2​(n!)=∑i≥1⌊n/2i⌋\mathrm{val}_{2}(n!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\lfloor n/2^{i}\rfloor, we also have

log2⁡(G⁡(n,1))=∑i≥1(⌊ni⌋−⌊n2i⌋−1).\log_{2}(G(n,1))=\sum_{i\geq 1}(\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{i}}\rfloor-1).

  1. (a)

    den⁡(n,x)=∏i=1n(1+xi)an,i\mathrm{den}(n,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+x^{i})^{a_{n,i}} with an,i=⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋+1a_{n,i}=\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor+1.

  2. (b)

    The maximal exponents αn,i\alpha_{n,i} such that (1+xi)αn,i|den⁡(n,x)(1+x^{i})^{\alpha_{n,i}}\mid\mathrm{den}(n,x) are αn,i=⌊ni⌋\alpha_{n,i}=\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor.

an,i=⌊ni⌋−cn,i=⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋+1.a_{n,i}=\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor-c_{n,i}=\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor+1\>.

βn,i=∑j≥1​ odd⌊ni⋅j⌋=γn,i+⌊ni⌋,\beta_{n,i}=\sum_{j\geq 1\textrm{ odd}}\lfloor\frac{n}{i\cdot j}\rfloor=\gamma_{n,i}+\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor\>,

where γn,i\gamma_{n,i} are the corresponding exponents of G⁡(n,x)G(n,x) (see Lemma 3.1). This determines the maximal exponents αn,i\alpha_{n,i} such that (1+xi)αn,i|den⁡(n,x)(1+x^{i})^{\alpha_{n,i}}\mid\mathrm{den}(n,x) are

αn,i=βn,i−γn,i=⌊ni⌋.\alpha_{n,i}=\beta_{n,i}-\gamma_{n,i}=\lfloor\frac{n}{i}\rfloor\>.

∎

Proposition 3.9.

Let nn be a positive integer. Then

  1. (a)

    G⁡(n,x)G(n,x), num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x), and den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) are palindromic.

  2. (b)

    den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) and G⁡(n,x)G(n,x) are unimodal.

Proof.

(a) Using Remark 3 (a), the statement follows from (3), Proposition 3.8 and the definition of num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x).

(b) For all mm, the product r⁡(m,x)=∏i=1m(1+xi)r(m,x)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1+x^{i}) is palindromic and unimodal (see e.g., [4], [6]). Recall that the exponents an,i=⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋+1a_{n,i}=\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor+1 of den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) are weakly decreasing (Proposition 3.8 (a)). The same holds for the exponents cn,ic_{n,i} of G⁡(n,x)G(n,x) (Proposition 3.5 (b)). So den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x), respectively G⁡(n,x)G(n,x), is the product of some r⁡(m,x)r(m,x). Then the statement follows from Remark 3. ∎

Next, we consider the quotient

𝔮​d​(n,x):=den⁡(n,x)den⁡(n−1,x).\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x):=\frac{\mathrm{den}(n,x)}{\mathrm{den}(n-1,x)}.
Proposition 3.10.

Let n≥2n\geq 2. Then

𝔮​d​(n,x)=∏k=0val2​(n)(1+x2k​𝐨​(n))=∏d|nΦ2​d​(x).\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x)=\prod_{k=0}^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)}(1+x^{2^{k}\mathbf{o}(n)})=\prod_{d\mid n}{\Phi_{2d}(x)}\>.

Moreover, deg⁡𝔮​d​(n,x)=2​n−𝐨⁡(n)\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x)=2n-\mathbf{o}(n).

Proof.

We have

∏d|n(1+xd)=den∗​(n,x)den∗​(n−1,x)=𝔮​G​(n,x)⋅𝔮​d​(n,x).\prod_{d\mid n}(1+x^{d})=\frac{\mathrm{den}^{\ast}(n,x)}{\mathrm{den}^{\ast}(n-1,x)}=\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}G}(n,x)\cdot\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x).

Then,

𝔮​d​(n,x)=∏k=0val2​(n)(1+x2k​𝐨​(n))=∏d|nΦ2​d​(x),\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x)=\prod_{k=0}^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)}(1+x^{2^{k}\mathbf{o}(n)})=\prod_{d\mid n}{\Phi_{2d}(x)}\>,

where the first equality above follows from Proposition 3.3 and the second from (1).

The degree is

deg⁡𝔮​d​(n,x)=∑k=0val2​(n)2k​𝐨​(n)=2​n−𝐨⁡(n).\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)}2^{k}\mathbf{o}(n)=2n-\mathbf{o}(n).

∎

There are various ways to calculate the degree of den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x), which leads to several equivalent formulas that, in turn, yield nice sum identities:

Let s⁡(n)s(n) be the sequence defined recursively for n≥1n\geq 1 by

s⁡(2​n)=s⁡(n)+2​n​ and ​s​(2​n−1)=2​n−1.s(2n)=s(n)+2n\textrm{ \ \ \ and\ \ \ }s(2n-1)=2n-1.

This is sequence A​129527\mathrm{A}\hskip-0.42677pt129527 in [5]. This sequence also appears in the generating function for the number PL⁡(n)\mathrm{PL}(n) of plane partitions of nn (see [3]):

∑n≥0PL⁡(n)​xn=∏(1+xn)s⁡(n).\sum_{n\geq 0}\mathrm{PL}(n)x^{n}=\prod(1+x^{n})^{s(n)}.
Corollary 3.11.

For n≥2n\geq 2, deg⁡𝔮​d​(n,x)=s⁡(n)\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x)=s(n).

Proof.

By Proposition 3.10, deg⁡𝔮​d​(2​m+1,x)=2​m+1\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(2m+1,x)=2m+1 and

deg⁡𝔮​d​(2​m,x)=4​m−𝐨⁡(m)=deg⁡𝔮​d​(m,x)+2​m.\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(2m,x)=4m-\mathbf{o}(m)=\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(m,x)+2m\>.

∎

Proposition 3.12.

Let n≥1n\geq 1. Then

deg⁡den⁡(n,x)=∑i=1ns⁡(i)=n⁡(n+1)−∑i=1n𝐨⁡(i)=n⁡(n+1)2+∑i=1ni⁡⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋;\deg\mathrm{den}(n,x)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}s(i)=n(n+1)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{o}(i)=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}i\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor\>;
deg⁡num⁡(n,x)=n2−∑i=1n𝐨⁡(i)=n⁡(n−1)2+∑i=1ni⁡⌊log2⁡(ni)⌋.\deg\mathrm{num}(n,x)=n^{2}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{o}(i)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}i\lfloor\lb(\frac{n}{i})\rfloor\>.
Proof.

Since

deg⁡den⁡(n,x)=1+∑i=2ndeg⁡𝔮​d​(i,x),\deg\mathrm{den}(n,x)=1+\sum_{i=2}^{n}\deg\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(i,x)\>,

the first two equalities for deg⁡den⁡(n,x)\deg\mathrm{den}(n,x) follow from Corollary 3.11 and Proposition 3.10 respectively. For the third equality, we use Proposition 3.8 (a). Finally, by definition deg⁡num⁡(n,x)=deg⁡den⁡(n,x)−n\deg\mathrm{num}(n,x)=\deg\mathrm{den}(n,x)-n. ∎

Remark 5.

We can now see that Conjecture 1 implies Conjecture 2. If num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x) is irreducible, then gcd⁡(num⁡(n,x),den⁡(n,x))\gcd\bigl(\mathrm{num}(n,x),\mathrm{den}(n,x)\bigr) must be either 11 or num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x). However, den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) is a ratio of (1+xi)(1+x^{i})’s, thus its irreducible factors are among the cyclotomic polynomials Φ2​d\Phi_{2d}, d≤nd\leq n. Hence, if gcd⁡(num⁡(n,x),den⁡(n,x))=num⁡(n,x)\gcd\bigl(\mathrm{num}(n,x),\mathrm{den}(n,x)\bigr)=\mathrm{num}(n,x), then num⁡(n,x)=Φ2​d\mathrm{num}(n,x)=\Phi_{2d} for some d≤nd\leq n, which contradicts the degree considerations of Proposition 3.12.

Proposition 3.13.

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

  1. (a)

    den⁡(n,1)=2val2​((2​n)!)\mathrm{den}(n,1)=2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}((2n)!)},

  2. (b)

    num⁡(n,1)=2val2​(n!)​P​(n)\mathrm{num}(n,1)=2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n!)}P(n).

Proof.

(a) For n=1n=1 the claim is obvious. For n>1n>1 we have the recursion den⁡(n,x)=𝔮​d​(n,x)​den​(n−1,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x)=\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n-1,x). Then, using induction and the explicit formula in Proposition (3.10), we have

den⁡(n,1)=𝔮​d​(n,1)​den​(n−1,1)=2val2​(n)+1⋅2val2​((2​n−2)!).\mathrm{den}(n,1)=\mathrm{\mathfrak{q}d}(n,1)\mathrm{den}(n-1,1)=2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)+1}\cdot 2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}((2n-2)!)}.

Since val2​(n)+1=val2​(2​n)+val2​(2​n−1)\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)+1=\mathrm{val}_{2}(2n)+\mathrm{val}_{2}(2n-1), the claim follows.

(b) For any λ\lambda, we have hλ​(1)=2∑i=1n⌊n/i⌋−nh_{\lambda}(1)=2^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lfloor n/i\rfloor-n}. Then, using Corollary 3.7, we have

num⁡(n,1)\displaystyle\mathrm{num}(n,1) =P⁡(n)⋅2∑i=1n⌊n/i⌋−nG⁡(n,1)=P⁡(n)⋅2val2​(n!).\displaystyle=\frac{P(n)\cdot 2^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lfloor n/i\rfloor-n}}{G(n,1)}=P(n)\cdot 2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n!)}\>.

∎

Example 1.

We write (am,μ)(a^{m},\mu) for a partition with largest part equal to aa and repeated mm times, and the remaining smaller parts forming a partition μ\mu. Given a partition λ\lambda, we define

Then num⁡(n,x)=∑λ⊢nqλ​(x)\mathrm{num}(n,x)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}q_{\lambda}(x).

To simplify the arguments, we introduce the following notation. For positive integers n,dn,d, and remainder r=n−d​⌊nd⌋r=n-d\lfloor\frac{n}{d}\rfloor, we define

Lemma 3.14.

and the result follows from (a).

We deduce a partial result related to Conjecture 2:

Corollary 3.15.

Fix n≥1n\geq 1 and d≥1d\geq 1, and let r=n−d​⌊nd⌋r=n-d\lfloor\frac{n}{d}\rfloor. Then

Φ2​d​(x)∤num⁡(n,x)\Phi_{2d}(x)\nmid\mathrm{num}(n,x)

Concerning Conjecture 2, gcd⁡(num⁡(n,x),den⁡(n,x))\gcd(\mathrm{num}(n,x),\mathrm{den}(n,x)) is at most a product of Φ2​d|(1+xi)\Phi_{2d}\mid(1+x^{i}), i≤ni\leq n. Moreover, Corollary 3.15 excludes some Φ2​d\Phi_{2d}. It is natural to search for zeros of num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x) on the unit circle, that is, to use methods similar to the circle method. Some experimental evidence shows that there are many roots of num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x) on the unit circle. However, we could not find any ζ2​d\zeta_{2d} among them. This can already be observed for small nn from Example 1: the roots of num⁡(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x) are on the unit circle for n≤3n\leq 3, the roots of num⁡(4,x)\mathrm{num}(4,x) are not on the unit circle, and ten zeros of num⁡(5,x)\mathrm{num}(5,x) are on the unit circle.

In general, the expression in Proposition 3.17 does not simplify as nicely as in Theorem 3.18.

We conclude this section with the following two conjectures for which we have experimental evidence.

Conjecture 3.

Write num⁡(n,x)=num0​(n,x)+num1​(n,x)\mathrm{num}(n,x)=\mathrm{num}_{0}(n,x)+\mathrm{num}_{1}(n,x) as the sum of an even and an odd function. Then num0​(n,x)\mathrm{num}_{0}(n,x) is unimodal.

Conjecture 4.

The sequence of coefficients of den⁡(n,x)\mathrm{den}(n,x) is log-concave except for n=3,5,6,7n=3,5,6,7.

4. Binary partitions

Let ℬ⁡(n)\mathcal{B}(n) denote the set of binary partitions of nn, that is, partitions whose parts are powers of 22. We set B⁡(n)=|ℬ⁡(n)|B(n)=|\mathcal{B}(n)|.

    d⁡(n)=2​(d⁡(⌊n2⌋)+⌊n2⌋).d(n)=2\left(d(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)+\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor\right).
  3. (c)

    If n=∑iai​2in=\sum_{i}a_{i}2^{i} is the binary representation of nn, then

    d⁡(n)=∑ii⋅ai​2i.d(n)=\sum_{i}i\cdot a_{i}2^{i}.
Remark 10.

The recurrence (b) computes d⁡(n)d(n) in log2⁡(n)\lb(n) steps. The expressions in (b) and (c) are given without proof in [5, A136013] (for the sequence d⁡(n)/2d(n)/2).

Proof.

(a) For n=2​m≥2n=2m\geq 2,

d⁡(n)=deg⁡ℋ2​(2​m,x)\displaystyle d(n)=\deg\mathcal{H}_{2}(2m,x) =deg⁡f2​m​(x)+deg⁡numℬ​(2​m−2,x)\displaystyle=\deg f_{2m}(x)+\deg\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(2m-2,x)
=2val2​(n)+1−2−d⁡(n−2).\displaystyle=2^{\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)+1}-2-d(n-2)\>.

(b) First assume n=2​mn=2m to be even. Then

d⁡(n)=deg⁡ℋ1​(2​m,x)\displaystyle d(n)=\deg\mathcal{H}_{1}(2m,x) =deg⁡(1+x)2​m+deg⁡numℬ​(m,x2)\displaystyle=\deg(1+x)^{2m}+\deg\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(m,x^{2})
=2​m+2​d​(m)=2​(d⁡(n2)+n2).\displaystyle=2m+2d(m)=2\left(d(\frac{n}{2})+\frac{n}{2}\right)\>.

For nn odd, d⁡(n)=d⁡(n−1)d(n)=d(n-1) and ⌊n2⌋=⌊n−12⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor=\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor, which completes the proof.

(c) This follows by induction using (b). ∎

Next, we give some evidence for the main conjecture of this section, which we rephrase below.

Conjecture 7.

For all n≥2n\geq 2 and for all 2i≤n2^{i}\leq n we have

(1+x2i)∤numℬ​(n,x).(1+x^{2^{i}})\nmid\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x).
Proposition 4.9.

Conjecture 5 is equivalent to Conjecture 7.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1, the polynomials (1+x2i)(1+x^{2^{i}}) are irreducible for all i≥0i\geq 0. Thus, denℬ​(n,x)=∏i≥0(1+x2i)⌊n/2i⌋\mathrm{den}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x)=\prod_{i\geq 0}(1+x^{2^{i}})^{\lfloor n/2^{i}\rfloor} is the decomposition of denℬ​(n,x)\mathrm{den}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x) into irreducible factors. Hence, any irreducible factor of gcd⁡(denℬ​(n,x),numℬ​(n,x))\gcd(\mathrm{den}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x),\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x)) must be of the form (1+x2i)(1+x^{2^{i}}) for 2i≤n2^{i}\leq n. ∎

Theorem 4.10.

Conjecture 7 holds for n=2kn=2^{k} and n=2k+1n=2^{k}+1 for k≥0.k\geq 0.

Proof.

If n=2kn=2^{k}, and i≤ki\leq k then ⌊n/2i⌋=2k−i\lfloor n/2^{i}\rfloor=2^{k-i}. Let λ∈ℬ⁡(2k)\lambda\in\mathcal{B}(2^{k}) be the partition with 2k−i2^{k-i} parts all equal to 2i2^{i}. Then (1+x2i)∤hλ​(x)(1+x^{2^{i}})\nmid h_{\lambda}(x). However, (1+x2i)|hμ​(x)(1+x^{2^{i}})\mid h_{\mu}(x) for all μ≠λ\mu\neq\lambda. Hence, (1+x2i)∤numℬ​(2k,x)(1+x^{2^{i}})\nmid\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(2^{k},x). The statement for n=2k+1n=2^{k}+1 follows from Proposition 4.1 (a). ∎

As in Lemma 3.14, (1+x2i)|numℬ​(n,x)(1+x^{2^{i}})\mid\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x) if and only if (1+x2i)|numℬ​(r,x)(1+x^{2^{i}})\mid\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(r,x), where r=n−2i​⌊n2i⌋r=n-2^{i}\lfloor\frac{n}{2^{i}}\rfloor. Then, one can show that for n≥2n\geq 2, (1+x2i)∤numℬ​(n,x)(1+x^{2^{i}})\nmid\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x) for i=0,1i=0,1 and 22.

5. Sums of powers of subsum polynomials

Let β⁡(n,x,m)=∑λ⊢nsp​(λ,x)m\beta(n,x,m)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)^{m}. So far we have studied β⁡(n,x,−1)=sr⁡(n,x)\beta(n,x,-1)=\mathrm{sr}(n,x).

Let Pk​(n)P_{k}(n) be the number of partitions of nn into kk sorts of parts; the order does not matter for parts of different sizes, but it does matter for parts of the same size and of different sorts. For example, for n=3n=3 and k=2k=2, the 1414 partitions are

(3a),(3b),(2a,1a),(2a,1b),(2b,1a),(2b,1b),(3_{a}),(3_{b}),(2_{a},1_{a}),(2_{a},1_{b}),(2_{b},1_{a}),(2_{b},1_{b}),
(1a,1a,1a),(1b,1a,1a),(1a,1b,1a),(1a,1a,1b),(1a,1b,1b),(1_{a},1_{a},1_{a}),(1_{b},1_{a},1_{a}),(1_{a},1_{b},1_{a}),(1_{a},1_{a},1_{b}),(1_{a},1_{b},1_{b}),
(1b,1a,1b),(1b,1b,1a),(1b,1b,1b).(1_{b},1_{a},1_{b}),(1_{b},1_{b},1_{a}),(1_{b},1_{b},1_{b}).

(See A246935 in [5].)

Proposition 5.1.

For n≥1n\geq 1,

  1. (a)

    β⁡(n,1,m)=P2m​(n)\beta(n,1,m)=P_{2^{m}}(n),

  2. (b)

    β⁡(2​n,−1,m)=P2m​(n)\beta(2n,-1,m)=P_{2^{m}}(n) and β⁡(2​n−1,−1,m)=0\beta(2n-1,-1,m)=0.

Proof.

(a) First note that sp⁡(λ,1)=∏i=1n2mλ​(i)=2∑mλ​(i)=2ℓ⁡(λ)\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,1)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}2^{m_{\lambda}(i)}=2^{\sum m_{\lambda}(i)}=2^{\ell(\lambda)}, where ℓ⁡(λ)\ell(\lambda) is the number of parts of λ\lambda. Hence,

β⁡(n,1,m)=∑λ⊢n2m​ℓ​(λ).\beta(n,1,m)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}2^{m\ell(\lambda)}.

To see that this equals P2m​(n)P_{2^{m}}(n), notice that from each ordinary partition λ\lambda of nn (that is, a partition with parts of a single sort), we can create 2m​ℓ​(λ)2^{m\ell(\lambda)} partitions with 2m2^{m} sorts of parts. There are 2m2^{m} choices for the sorts for the first part, 2m2^{m} choices for the sorts for the second part, etc.

(b) If λ\lambda has an odd part, then sp⁡(λ,−1)=0\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,-1)=0. If 𝒫e​(n)\mathcal{P}_{e}(n) is the set of partitions of nn with all parts even, then

β⁡(n,−1,m)=∑λ∈𝒫e​(n)sp​(λ,−1)m.\beta(n,-1,m)=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{e}(n)}\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,-1)^{m}.

Since all partitions of 2​n−12n-1 have at least one odd part, β⁡(2​n−1,−1,m)=0\beta(2n-1,-1,m)=0.

The transformation λ→λ/2\lambda\to\lambda/2 is a bijection from 𝒫e​(2​n)\mathcal{P}_{e}(2n) to the set of all partitions of nn. If λ∈𝒫e​(2​n)\lambda\in\mathcal{P}_{e}(2n), we have sp⁡(λ,−1)=sp⁡(λ,1)=sp⁡(λ/2,1).\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,-1)=\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,1)=\mathrm{sp}(\lambda/2,1). Thus β⁡(2​n,−1,m)=β⁡(n,1,m)\beta(2n,-1,m)=\beta(n,1,m) and the result follows from (a). ∎

Proposition 5.2.

Let n≥1n\geq 1 and denote by β′​(n,x,m)\beta^{\prime}(n,x,m) the derivative of β⁡(n,x,m)\beta(n,x,m) with respect to xx. Then

val2​(β′​(n,1,k))=val2​(n)+val2​(k)+k−1.\mathrm{val}_{2}(\beta^{\prime}(n,1,k))=\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)+\mathrm{val}_{2}(k)+k-1.
Proof.

We have

β′​(n,x,k)=∑λ⊢nk⋅sp​(λ,x)k−1​sp′​(λ,x).\beta^{\prime}(n,x,k)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}k\cdot\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)^{k-1}\mathrm{sp}^{\prime}(\lambda,x).

Using logarithmic differentiation, we have

sp′​(λ,x)=sp⁡(λ,x)​∑i=1nmλ​(i)​i​xi−11+xi.\mathrm{sp}^{\prime}(\lambda,x)=\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x)\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{\lambda}(i)\frac{ix^{i-1}}{1+x^{i}}.

Evaluating at x=1x=1, we obtain

β′​(n,1,k)\displaystyle\beta^{\prime}(n,1,k) =∑λ⊢nk⋅sp(λ,1)k∑i=1nmλ(i)i2=12nk∑λ⊢n2k​ℓ​(λ)=12nk2k∑λ⊢n2k⁡(ℓ⁡(λ)−1).\displaystyle=\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}k\cdot\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,1)^{k}\sum_{i=1}^{n}m_{\lambda}(i)\frac{i}{2}=\frac{1}{2}nk\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}2^{k\ell(\lambda)}=\frac{1}{2}nk2^{k}\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}2^{k(\ell(\lambda)-1)}.

Since λ=(n)\lambda=(n) is the only partition of nn with ℓ⁡(λ)=1\ell(\lambda)=1, it follows that ∑λ⊢n2k⁡(ℓ⁡(λ)−1)\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}2^{k(\ell(\lambda)-1)} is odd. Hence, val2​(β′​(n,1,k))=val2​(n)+val2​(k)+k−1.\mathrm{val}_{2}(\beta^{\prime}(n,1,k))=\mathrm{val}_{2}(n)+\mathrm{val}_{2}(k)+k-1. ∎

6. Open Questions

Analogously to srℬ​(n,x)\mathrm{sr}_{\mathcal{B}}(n,x) for the binary partitions of nn, we can define s​r𝒜​(n,x)sr_{\mathcal{A}}(n,x) for any subset 𝒜⁡(n)\mathcal{A}(n) of partitions of nn and study the questions posed in this article. We offer the following conjectures.

Let 𝒪⁡(n)\mathcal{O}(n) be the set of odd partitions of nn, that is, partitions whose parts are all odd.

Conjecture 8.

For n≥1n\geq 1, num𝒪​(n,−1)=𝐨⁡(n!)\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{O}}(n,-1)=\mathbf{o}(n!).

Let 𝒯⁡(n)\mathcal{T}(n) be the set of ternary partitions of nn, that is, partitions whose parts are powers of 33.

Conjecture 9.

Let s⁡(n)=num𝒯​(n,−1)s(n)=\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{T}}(n,-1). Then s⁡(1)=s⁡(2)=1s(1)=s(2)=1 and s⁡(3​n)=s⁡(3​n+1)=s⁡(3​n+2)=3val3​((3​n)!)s(3n)=s(3n+1)=s(3n+2)=3^{\mathrm{val}_{3}((3n)!)}.

Conjecture 10.

Let t⁡(n)=num𝒯​(n,1)t(n)=\mathrm{num}_{\mathcal{T}}(n,1). Then t⁡(1)=t⁡(2)=1t(1)=t(2)=1 and t⁡(3​n)=t⁡(3​n+1)=t⁡(3​n+2)t(3n)=t(3n+1)=t(3n+2). Also, t⁡(n)=Δ⁡(t⁡(3​n−2)/22​n)t(n)=\Delta(t(3n-2)/2^{2n}).

Finally, we note that one can replace xix^{i} in sp⁡(λ,x)\mathrm{sp}(\lambda,x) and sr⁡(n,x)\mathrm{sr}(n,x) by xi¯x^{\overline{i}} or xi¯x^{\underline{i}}, where i¯\overline{i} and i¯\underline{i}, are the rising and falling factorials, respectively. Conjecturally, these polynomials have interesting properties, and we hope the interested reader will explore them.
